prize_parts.citation: For the invention of the optical lattice clock based on magic-wavelength trapping and its development to the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single prize for the optical lattice clock to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. Reading the full exchange sharpened the scope rather than the choice. The achievement is a specific, attributable invention. Katori's magic-wavelength trapping removes Doppler, recoil and light-shift errors for many atoms at once, and the Ye group's work showed that the idea reaches roughly 1e-18 with controlled many-body and density effects. That is what separates it from the 2005 prize, which honoured the frequency comb and precision laser spectroscopy, and from the 2012 prize, which honoured control of single trapped ions. The lattice clock interrogates a neutral-atom ensemble and gets its statistical power from the ensemble, which is a different route from either. Maturity is not in doubt: independent laboratories in several countries intercompare at this level, and no member has raised a reproducibility concern. The chair asks whether the clock should be framed as invention or capability. I would frame it as an invention that has already enabled new measurements, namely tests of constants and relativistic redshift at millimetre-to-centimetre height differences, and I would keep the citation to the concept and its realisation, not to precision spectroscopy in general. I do not rely on the seven-of-eight count. It is a signal that the case survived scrutiny, and the merit argument stands without it.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is still category and credit. Some of the committee will call this an instrument advance, and the largest consequences, a redefinition of the second, chronometric geodesy and drift or dark-matter searches, are mostly prospective. Danielsson's point that twisted bilayer graphene produced a surprising new phenomenon within a year is a fair contrast, and if the committee decides that discovery of a new phenomenon must outweigh a measurement invention this year, B025 loses and B022 should lead. On credit, Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Sterr and Gill made real contributions to the early strontium and ytterbium demonstrations and to the stability record, and a two-name list cannot hold them. The statutes allow three, but I do not see a third name whose claim is as clear as these two, so I would rather leave the citation narrow than invent a third. I also have not verified the 1e-18 figures or the chronology of the first lattice clocks against primary papers and flag that again.

responses.point: Danielsson is the only member who prefers B022 (magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene), framing the choice as a surprising new phenomenon against an extraordinary but largely prospective measurement capability, and argues Bistritzer must stay in the credit.
responses.response: I agree with him on Bistritzer: the 2011 continuum-model paper is a two-author prediction and a list without its first author would be wrong, so if B022 advances it should be the three names I proposed. I also share his view that the pairing mechanism should not by itself disqualify the case, since a citation worded around the prediction and the observation claims no mechanism. Where I part from him is the weight on discovery versus capability. The criterion I quoted in March is discovery or invention, and the lattice clock is a clear invention with consequences nobody could test before it. The maturity profiles also differ. Cross-laboratory agreement for the clock is quantitative and stable. For B022 the sample and twist-angle dependence still make comparison between groups difficult after about eight years. I hold B022 as my first alternative and I would not oppose it in a later year.

responses.point: Lindroth wants the citation and deliberation to acknowledge Lemonde, the SYRTE group and the ion-clock lineage, and says that the electron-microscope corrector is an enabling tool whose payoff is spread across materials science, whereas clocks feed back into fundamental physics.
responses.response: The second point is fair and it is why I no longer press B008 as a preferred configuration. Aberration correction changed what can be seen in materials and chemistry, but the physics it uniquely enabled is harder to name in one sentence than for the clock. On credit, I agree the deliberation should record the SYRTE and early strontium contributions. I would handle it in the citation wording, which should name the magic-wavelength lattice clock and its performance at 1e-18 and make no claim for the whole field of optical clocks. I would not add Lemonde as a third laureate, because a third name would need a clear distinct claim and I cannot identify one from the record.

responses.point: Kroll holds that the committee has recognised measurement inventions before (Charpak, Hall and Haensch), that Ye should be credited once for the lattice clock because the thorium nuclear clock is not yet competitive, and he disclosed a research stay in John Hall's laboratory.
responses.response: I accept the precedent argument, and I rely on the same line for the lattice clock: measurement inventions have been recognised when they changed what could be tested. I also agree that the thorium-229 work is not a competitor for the credit. Nuclear clocks have not matched lattice performance, so Ye is credited once, for the lattice clock. On his disclosure, a stay in Hall's laboratory is a lineage tie to the 2005 prize and no collaboration with Katori or Ye is documented. I do not see it as requiring recusal. I would ask him to say plainly whether he has any joint work with Ye, so the committee can record the answer, and I note that it is for the committee and not for either of us to judge it.

responses.point: Pearce asks whether the citation should be written around the lattice clock and its accuracy and not around spectroscopy in general, whether Ye's role is accuracy and many-body programme or a distinct invention, and rejects pairing the clock with B037.
responses.response: I agree on the wording and I agree on B037. The citation should be about the lattice clock and its accuracy, and I would not link it to quantum simulation with ultracold atoms, which is a different achievement and would need four names. On Ye's role, I read it as more than a performance programme. Reaching 1e-18 required showing that the lattice could be operated with controlled collisional and many-body shifts and with very stable lasers, and that is part of the invention as realised, not a refinement of it. That is why my citation says development to the 10^-18 level, which keeps both names and does not claim the concept for Ye or the record for Katori. I would still welcome Lindroth's atomic-physics judgement on whether this wording is accurate.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats the lattice clock as an invention distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, or as an extension of them.
How much weight the early strontium and ytterbium contributions of Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Sterr and Gill should carry against the two-name credit.
Whether discovery of a new phenomenon (B022) should outrank a measurement invention with mainly prospective consequences.

The 1e-18 uncertainty figures, the chronology of the first lattice clocks and the exact roles of Katori and Ye are from recollection and should be checked against primary intercomparisons before the citation is fixed.
statement.conflict_note: I have a documented institutional connection to Japan through a JSPS fellowship, a University of Tokyo fellowship and long-running exchanges with Japanese universities. Hidetoshi Katori is, to my recollection, at the University of Tokyo, but nothing in my record documents a collaboration or co-authorship with him or with Jun Ye. I have no further disclosure on this point since round 1 and I leave the recusal judgement to the committee. I have discounted my own first-place B008 because it lies in my field of electron microscopy, and I no longer treat it as a preferred or alternative ballot. My Chalmers colleague Goran Johansson favours B016, which I do not prefer, and I see no conflict there.
